stories.title: Measles Cases in Singapore Hit a 6-Year High
stories.headline_kid: Doctors have found 40 cases of measles in Singapore this year — the most since 2020 — so parents are being reminded to check everyone's jabs.
summary: Singapore has recorded 40 cases of measles so far this year. That is the highest number in six years! Measles is a disease caused by a virus that spreads very easily through the air, almost like how a cold spreads when someone coughs near you.

The tricky part is that even three people who were already vaccinated still caught measles. But doctors say this does not mean the vaccine does not work — it just means no vaccine gives 100% protection all the time. Most people in Singapore are still well protected because our vaccination rates are high.

Measles causes fever, a red rash, and a bad cough. It can be more serious for babies who are too young to be vaccinated yet. That is why health experts are reminding parents to make sure their children's vaccination records are up to date.

Experts say Singapore is not likely to see a huge outbreak because so many of us are already vaccinated. Around the world, measles cases are rising in places where fewer people get vaccinated, so Singapore is keeping a close watch.

lenses.me: If you feel feverish with a rash, tell an adult quickly — and check with your parents if your own vaccinations (like MMR) are complete.
lenses.family: Parents may want to check their children's vaccination booklets, especially before travelling overseas.
lenses.friends: If a classmate is unwell with a fever and rash, your school may ask them to stay home so it does not spread to others.
lenses.nation: Singapore's health system tracks diseases like measles closely so outbreaks can be stopped early, keeping everyone safer.
lenses.world: Measles cases are rising in many countries because fewer people are getting vaccinated, showing why vaccines matter globally.

stories.title: Shanti Pereira Races Into History at the Commonwealth Games!
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's fastest woman just made history by qualifying for the 200m final at the Commonwealth Games!
summary: Singapore sprinter Shanti Pereira has done something no Singaporean has done before — she qualified for the women's 200m final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. She ran a season-best time of 22.81 seconds in her semi-final race.
The Commonwealth Games is a huge sports competition, a bit like a mini-Olympics, where athletes from countries that used to be part of the British Empire compete against each other every four years.
Shanti has been Singapore's top sprinter for years, and this achievement shows how far she has come. Reaching a final at this level means she is now among the fastest women in the whole Commonwealth.

Many Singaporeans are excited and proud, cheering her on as she prepares to race for a medal in the final. Her journey shows that with hard work and determination, small nations can still shine on the world stage.

lenses.me: Watching an athlete from your own country do so well can inspire you to work hard at something you love, like sports or a hobby.
lenses.family: Your family might gather to watch her final race together, cheering for Singapore.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates might talk about her achievement during recess or PE lessons.
lenses.nation: Shanti's success puts Singapore on the map in world athletics and could inspire more young Singaporeans to take up track and field.
lenses.world: Her achievement shows that athletes from smaller countries can still compete with, and beat, bigger sporting nations.

stories.title: Japan Earthquake Deaths Rise to 34 as Rescuers Battle the Heat
stories.headline_kid: The death toll from Japan's big earthquake has more than doubled, and rescuers are now racing against the hot weather too.
summary: The number of people who died after the powerful earthquake in Kumamoto, Japan, has risen sharply to 34. Just two days ago, the toll was 13 — showing how serious the damage really was.

The earthquake, which struck with a magnitude of 7.1, caused a shopping mall called Aeon Mall in Kashima town to collapse. Many rescue workers are still digging through the rubble, hoping to find survivors trapped inside.
Rescuers now face another challenge: very hot weather. Working in the heat for hours makes searching harder and more tiring, but hundreds of workers are pushing on to try and save anyone still alive.

Japan is a popular place for Singaporean families to travel to for holidays. Events like this remind us why it's important to check travel advisories and stay updated on safety information before and during a trip.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a trip to Japan, this is a reminder to check news updates before you go.
lenses.family: Parents booking flights or holidays to Japan may want to follow official travel advisories closely.
lenses.friends: You might discuss with classmates how earthquakes happen and why some countries, like Japan, are more prone to them.
lenses.nation: Singapore often sends messages of support and sometimes aid to countries hit by disasters like this.
lenses.world: This tragedy reminds the world how powerful and unpredictable earthquakes can be, especially in countries built along fault lines.

stories.title: Fighting Near an Important Sea Route Could Push Up Petrol Prices
stories.headline_kid: The US and Iran are still fighting near a narrow sea passage that carries a huge share of the world's oil — and that could make petrol pricier here in Singapore.
summary: The United States and Iran have been attacking each other, and the fighting has spread near the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow strip of sea that ships use to carry oil from the Middle East to the rest of the world. Imagine a busy one-lane bridge that almost everyone must cross to deliver an important package — that's the Strait of Hormuz for oil.
Pakistan is trying to help both sides talk and calm things down, but the fighting has continued, with the US launching a 'heavy wave of strikes' recently.

When fighting happens near this important sea route, oil prices around the world often go up because companies worry about ships being unable to pass safely. Oil prices already jumped over 7% in just one day this week.

Singapore does not have its own oil, so we buy it from other countries. When oil becomes more expensive, it can make petrol, bus and taxi fares, and even everyday goods slightly more costly for families here.

lenses.me: Higher oil prices might mean your family spends a bit more on transport or things made using oil-based materials, like plastic toys.
lenses.family: Parents may notice petrol prices creeping up when filling up the car.
lenses.friends: Not a direct effect on friends, but it's a good topic to discuss during class discussions about world events.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies heavily on imported oil, so instability in the Middle East can affect our fuel and transport costs.
lenses.world: Many countries around the world depend on oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz, so conflict there can shake economies globally.

stories.title: Samsung's Profits Rocket Up 1,800% Thanks to AI Boom
stories.headline_kid: Samsung, the company that makes chips inside your phone and computer, just made 19 times more profit — all because of the AI boom!
summary: Samsung Electronics, a giant tech company from South Korea, announced its profits shot up by an incredible 1,800% compared to last year. That means the company made 19 times more money than before!

The reason is artificial intelligence, or AI. Big tech companies around the world are building powerful AI computers, called data centres, and these need special memory chips to work — the exact chips Samsung makes.
Think of memory chips like a brain's storage space. The more powerful the AI, the more storage and speed it needs, so companies are buying huge amounts of chips from Samsung.

This AI boom affects more than just Samsung. Singapore is home to many chip and electronics factories too, so when demand for chips rises worldwide, it can create more jobs and business opportunities here as well.

lenses.me: The chips inside your phone, tablet, or gaming console are similar to what Samsung makes — this is why gadgets keep getting smarter!
lenses.family: Your family's electronics might become more advanced (or pricier) as chip demand grows.
lenses.friends: Classmates who love gadgets or gaming will find it interesting how AI is changing the tech industry.
lenses.nation: Singapore has its own chip-making factories, so a global chip boom can bring more business and jobs to our country.
lenses.world: The AI boom is reshaping economies worldwide, showing how technology can change which companies and countries become powerful.
